text:
This tutorial
In this tutorial, we demonstrate forecasting the 2020Q1 CPI level, including stationarity tests, ARIMA model selection, and the final forecast computation.










Agenda



Exercise 1(a): Transform CPI levels into log differences and select the ADF specification (lags).
Exercise 1(b): Test the log-differenced series for a unit root (ADF).
Exercise 1(c): Select the ARIMA model using AICc and Ljung–Box diagnostics.
Exercise 1(d): Forecast 2020Q1 inflation and the CPI level.
Exercise 2: Explain why first differencing removes a linear trend.

section: We know that taking the logs is not enough…
text:
We know that taking the logs is not enough…

Carry out an ADF test of Y, present (i) the estimated test equation, (ii) the \(t_{\text{ADF}}\) test statistic, 5% critical value and decision, and (iii) its \(p\)-value.





library(urca)    # For use of ur.df function
adf <- ur.df(Y, type = "trend", selectlags = "AIC")
p_adf <- punitroot(adf@teststat[1], trend = "ct", statistic = "t")





(i) test equation(ii) test summary(iii) \(p\)-value


The test equation is: \[\Delta Y_{t}=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}t+\varphi Y_{t-1}+\sum^{p-1}_{k=1}\psi_{k} \Delta Y_{t-k}+U_{t}\] The hypotheses are: \[\begin{align}
H_{0}:&\;\varphi=0& &\text{($Y_{t}$ has a unit root)}\\
H_{1}:&\;\varphi<0& &\text{($Y_{t}$ does not have a unit root)}
\end{align}\] The number of lags of \(\Delta Y_{t}\) (i.e., \(p-1\)) is selected by an information criterion (AIC), where \(p\) is the order of the underlying AR model.



summary(adf)


###############################################

############################################### 

Test regression trend

z.diff.lag   5.147e-01  5.049e-02  10.193   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.01025 on 290 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.3263,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.3193 
F-statistic: 46.82 on 3 and 290 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Value of test-statistic is: 0.099 16.8276 3.9857

      1pct  5pct 10pct
tau3 -3.98 -3.42 -3.13

print(p_adf)

[1] 0.9973104





Since \(p=0.997>0.05\), we fail to reject the null hypothesis \(H_{0}\): there is unit root.



\(\implies\) Simply removing the trend component is not enough to make \(Y_{t}\) stationary. 
\(\implies\) We need to take the first difference of log CPI.

text:
Exercise 1(c)

Specify and estimate an appropriate ARIMA(\(p,d,q\)) model for \(Y_{t}\).











Since first differencing is required for log CPI to be stationary, we need \(d=1\).
How to select \((p,q)\)? \(\to\) Conduct a grid search for \(p=0,\dots,4\) and \(q=0,\dots,4\)














Code Structure



Set up container matrices for AICc values (AICc) and Ljung-Box test \(p\)-values (LBp)
For each \((p,q)\) combination:

Fit the ARIMA(\(p,1,q\)) model with Arima() function, and extract AICc
Extract the Ljung-Box \(p\)-values with checkresiduals() function

Choose the model with the lowest AICc, and verify that its Ljung-Box \(H_{0}\) (no autocorrelation) is not rejected.

text:
Exercise 1(c)

Specify and estimate an appropriate ARIMA(\(p,d,q\)) model for \(Y_{t}\).











Since first differencing is required for log CPI to be stationary, we need \(d=1\).
How to select \((p,q)\)? \(\to\) Conduct a grid search for \(p=0,\dots,4\) and \(q=0,\dots,4\)





library(forecast)

pmax <- 4
qmax <- 4
LBp <- matrix(nrow=pmax+1, ncol=qmax+1)
rownames(LBp) <- paste0("p=", 0:pmax)
colnames(LBp) <- paste0("q=", 0:qmax)
AICc <- LBp

for (p in 0:pmax){
  for (q in 0:qmax){
    eq <- Arima(DY, order=c(p,0,q))
    capture.output(LBp[p+1,q+1] <- checkresiduals(eq,
      plot=FALSE)$p.value)
    AICc[p+1,q+1] <- eq$aicc
  }  
}

text:
Exercise 1(d)

Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020.










Note that we have selected ARMA(1,3) for \(\Delta Y_{t}\equiv \Delta\log(CPI_{t})\) in Exercise 1(c).







Forecast 2020Q1 inflation: \(\Delta{}Y_{2020Q1}=\log(CPI_{2020Q1})-\log(CPI_{2019Q4})\)

eq <- Arima(DY, order = c(1,0,3))
ForecastInflation_2020q1 <- forecast(eq, h=1)$mean
print(ForecastInflation_2020q1)

           Qtr1
2020 0.00710347







The inflation forecast is based on an approximation…
Recall from Week 1 tutorial that for small \(r\) values, \(\log(1+r)\approx r\): \[\begin{align}
CPI_{2019Q4}(1+\text{inflation}_{2020Q1})&=CPI_{2020Q1}\\
\log(1+\text{inflation}_{2020Q1})&=\log(CPI_{2020Q1})-\log(CPI_{2019Q4})\\
\implies\qquad \color{blue}{\text{inflation}_{2020Q1}}&\approx\log(CPI_{2020Q1})-\log(CPI_{2019Q4})
\end{align}\]

CPI_2019q4 <- CPI[which(time(CPI)==2019.75)]

# Forecast CPI for 2020q1

print(ForecastCPI_2020q1)

Recall that we modeled \(\Delta Y_{t}\) as ARMA(1,3) \(\Rightarrow\) \(Y_{t}\) should be modeled as ARMA(1,1,3).




ARIMA(1,1,3) for \(Y_{t}\equiv\log(CPI_{t})\)ARMA(1,3) for \(\Delta Y_{t}\equiv\Delta \log(CPI_{t})\)

Regression with ARIMA(1,1,3) errors

text:
Exercise 1(d)

Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020.




Remarks on the CPI forecasts:
Both approaches are approximations.



First approach: \(\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=CPI_{2019Q4}\times (1+\color{purple}{\underbrace{\widehat{\text{inflation}}_{2020Q1}}_{\text{approximation}}})\)



Second approach: \(\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=\exp(\color{teal}{\log(\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1})}\color{black}{)}\)




The inner part is an estimate of an expectation conditional on information set \(\mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}\): \[\widehat{\log(CPI_{2020Q1})}\equiv\hat{Y}_{2020Q1}=\hat{\mathbb{E}}[Y_{2020Q1}\mid \mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]\] 

\[\implies \widehat{\log(CPI_{2020Q1})}=\hat{\mathbb{E}}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid \mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]\] and this is estimated through the ARIMA(1,1,3) model fitted on \(Y_{t}\).

Tutor: Pengyun (Kevin) Chen


University of Melbourne


Semester 2, 2026
text:
Exercise 1(d)

Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020.




Remarks on the CPI forecasts:
Both approaches are approximations.



First approach: \(\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=CPI_{2019Q4}\times (1+\color{purple}{\underbrace{\widehat{\text{inflation}}_{2020Q1}}_{\text{approximation}}})\)



Second approach: \(\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=\exp(\color{blue}{\hat{\mathbb{E}}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid\mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]}\color{black}{)}\)



 Question: Does the following hold? \[\color{blue}{\mathbb{E}[{CPI}_{2020Q1}\mid\mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]\overset{?}{=}\exp(\mathbb{E}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid \mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}])}\] 

 Answer: No. This is because of Jensen’s inequality - since \(\exp(x)\) is convex: \[\mathbb{E}[\exp(\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid \mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4})]>\exp(\mathbb{E}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid \mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}])\]

text:
Exercise 1(d)

Use the chosen model to calculate a forecast of inflation and the CPI for the March quarter of 2020.




Remarks on the CPI forecasts:
Both approaches are approximations.



First approach: \(\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=CPI_{2019Q4}\times (1+\color{purple}{\underbrace{\widehat{\text{inflation}}_{2020Q1}}_{\text{approximation}}})\)



Second approach: \(\widehat{CPI}_{2020Q1}=\exp(\hat{\mathbb{E}}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid\mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]\color{black}{)}\)



 Thus this estimator is actually biased for the conditional mean \(\mathbb{E}[CPI_{2020Q1}\mid\mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]\): \[\mathbb{E}[CPI_{2020Q1}\mid\mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}]>\exp(\mathbb{E}[\log(CPI_{2020Q1})\mid \mathcal{Y}_{2019Q4}])\] 

 Nevertheless, in practice, simply taking the exponential tends to work well in providing a good approximation.

Exercise 2

It seems like if \(Y_{t}\) has a linear trend then \(\Delta Y_{t}\) does not. Explain why this is.










Show that \(\alpha=\beta_{1}\), \(W_{t}=\Delta Z_{t}\) in the following equations:
\[Y_{t}=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}t+Z_{t}\qquad\qquad\Delta Y_{t}=\alpha+W_{t}\]







Subtract \(Y_{t-1}\) on both sides gives:
\[Y_{t}\,\color{blue}{-\,Y_{t-1}}\color{black}{\,=(\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}t+Z_{t})}\color{blue}{\,-\,(\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}(t-1)+Z_{t-1})}\]


Then simplify: \[\begin{align*}

Y_{t}-Y_{t-1}&=\beta_{0}-\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}(t-(t-1))+Z_{t}-Z_{t-1}\\
\Delta Y_{t}&=\beta_{1}+\Delta Z_{t}
\end{align*}\]


We have thereby shown that \(\alpha=\beta_{1}\) and \(W_{t}=\Delta Z_{t}\).





In addition, we have shown that taking the first difference removes the linear trend.  \[Y_{t}=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}t+Z_{t}\quad\xrightarrow{\;\textsf{take first difference}\;}\quad \Delta Y_{t}=\beta_{1}+\Delta Z_{t}\]
